Africa has built much of the legal architecture for a continental market. The next border is inside the production system.

A tariff preference can cut one cost. It cannot make a truck move predictably, settle an invoice, certify a component, keep a factory powered or make two customs systems exchange data.

The World Bank’s August 2026 integration report estimates that only 15–20% of Africa’s total trade is intra-African and that around 60% of trade costs arise behind countries’ own borders. The next gains are increasingly operational.

East Africa’s Single Customs Territory and one-stop border posts have reduced transit frictions, but the next gains require smarter technology and fewer domestic bottlenecks.

West Africa has synchronized interconnected power systems and is preparing a day-ahead electricity market. PAPSS is extending local-currency payment connectivity. The Lobito Corridor governments have formally acknowledged that infrastructure alone is not enough and are linking logistics to processing, agribusiness, energy and SMEs. The Abidjan–Lagos highway is being structured as a single supranational asset rather than five disconnected national roads.

These are usually described as separate stories. StoneComms’ conclusion is that their value is multiplicative.

A regional production hub appears only when movement, power, payment, standards and governance work together well enough for a firm to distribute production across borders without rebuilding its operating model at each frontier.

We call this the Production Operating System.

Its five interfaces are:

MOVE — goods and people cross predictably.
POWER — energy can follow production.
PAY — money settles at the speed of commerce.
PROVE — products and professionals do not become “unknown” at each border.
GOVERN — someone owns the failures between institutions.

The policy goal is minimum viable interoperability: agree the interfaces that must work without forcing identical systems underneath.

That has a direct investment implication. DFIs and governments should ask whether a corridor is integration-complete, not merely asset-complete. A railway can reach commissioning while customs, standards, power access and payments still behave as national islands.

StoneComms proposes an Integration Covenant: measurable conditions around the interfaces that must function when the physical asset opens.

For corridor authorities, trade ministries, DFIs and investors, the strategic question is not simply “has the road or railway been built?” It is “can a firm actually produce across the markets it connects?”
